I was 27 when the 07-08 crash happened. I worked for a large mortgage lender at the time. I was hired as a temp to answer the phones when I was 20 during the refi boom and worked my way up through the ranks eventually becoming a Sales Rep. The hot items we sold were No Doc loans and 1% Option Arms. Being young and relatively new to this business I thought this was how mortgage loan programs worked and I thought nothing wrong of it. In 2007, over 250 banks imploded. My colleagues and I watched the implode o meter website every single day. The bank I worked for at the time assured us we were okay and that we wouldn’t go under but 8 months into the crash they couldn’t hold on and they shut down. I lost my job and so did many others and I could not find a job for over a year! My company did give us a severance package which helped for a couple months and then I had to go on unemployment. When I did find a job over a year later, I was making significantly less than what I was prior and it was like this for 5 years after, the jobs didn’t pay well. It finally started to turn around for the better in 2012 after all the 2010 regulations took place. Now 20-21 eerily feels like 07-08 again. The business is booming right now due to low interest rates and many are buying and refinancing. Home values are overinflated and I can’t find anything worth a crap for under 300k in my state that already has incredibly high property taxes. We also have many people currently unemployed due to covid and pausing their mortgage payments under the cares act. I’m curious to see how this all plays out in the next year or so. I’m really hoping it’s not a repeat of 07-08.

Edit to say - I love the company I work for now! I don’t want a repeat 😫

Robinhood makes money by selling your order to Citadel.

Citadel makes money by executing your order in a way advantageous to them.

Citadel loaned a bunch of money to Melvin Capital.

If Melvin Capital goes under, Citadel doesn't get their money.

Citadel tells Robinhood to stop allowing purchases of GME; to save Melvin.

Remember how Robinhood makes their money.

> The secret to Robinhood's success (and profitability) is simple: payment for order flow. **To ensure trades are commission free, trades are sold to "market makers'' or large firms such as Citadel Securities—Robinhood’s largest customer, which tried to bail out Melvin Capital after its Gamestop shorts cost it billions**. Market makers execute those trades (sometimes at an inferior rate) and can use their privileged position to place themselves in the middle and make a profit.

There's no such thing as a "free" service. In the Internet era, user information is a valuable currency - and we're all just giving it away for free.
